title: The Draw of Draws: Give Check to Become Stalemated
summary: Use the last pawn to force the opposing king onto the squares that lock your own king.

nodes.question: How can the last pawn force a draw against a queen?
nodes.explanation: g3+ attacks Kh4. Black must capture the pawn or step to h3; either king move covers White’s remaining flights while f2 controls g1. White then has no legal move and is not in check.

branches.title: Source finish: the king takes the checking pawn
commentary: Begin after ...gxf2. The black pawn on f2 came from g3, leaving g3 free for White’s last pawn. Black retains c6/d5/g4/g5/h5.
g3+ checks Kh4. The pawn’s advance is forcing; Black cannot simply make an unrelated queen move.
Kxg3 captures White’s last pawn. Kh1 cannot go to g1 because f2 attacks it, or to g2/h2 because Kg3 controls them. White is not in check and has no legal move: actual stalemate.

branches.title: Source alternative: the king steps to h3
commentary: Compare the other legal answer to the pawn check. Every pawn stays on the board in this branch.
g3+ forces a king response. Kh3 and Kxg3 are the only legal replies.
Kh3 leaves the white pawn blocked by g4. Kh1 cannot use g1 because of f2, or g2/h2 because Kh3 controls them. White is not in check, so this is actual stalemate too.

exercises.prompt: Why must Black answer with the king?
exercises.answer: The adjacent pawn check cannot be blocked. No black piece can capture g3 except Kh4, leaving just Kxg3 and Kh3.

exercises.prompt: Is one illustrated stalemate enough to prove the root drawn?
exercises.answer: No. White must be able to avoid losing, and Black must be able to prevent a White win. Separate complete legal strategies establish both for this selected diagram.

startContext: Begin after ...gxf2 at 166 seconds in the complete ten-piece later diagram: White Kh1/g2 against Kh4/Qf8/c6/d5/f2/g4/g5/h5. The source g3+ forces either Kxg3 or Kh3, both actual stalemates with every pawn retained until the shown capture. Exact draw verification supplies separate finite non-loss strategies for White and Black: White forces these stalemates; Black’s independent Qf4+ responses to Kh2 prevent a White win through complete legal mate/stalemate leaves. This proves the selected root drawn, not merely one sampled stalemate. The earlier eleven-plus-piece bishop fortress, queen captures and knight sacrifice remain outside this proof.
